near_miss.lead: orð ... flytia til eyrna: carrying words to ears
near_miss.why_not: Thucydides partner only has hearing a sustained speech. Search finds Sophocles Ajax 148–149 with words carried into ears, recorded separately as a search lead, but not a second slab anchor.

search_lead.cognate: ON eyrna (eyra, genitive plural governed by til) and Greek ὦτα (accusative plural after εἰς) continue the ear noun *h₂ous-.
search_lead.argument: Both construe spoken words as things conveyed to ears: diplomatic delivery versus circulation of whispered allegations. flytia renews the carrying verb; orð and λόγους are not cognate. A possible inherited metaphor for review, with only one cognate noun and substantial risk of independent idiom.

near_miss.lead: orð bera / uerba ... dicta referre: carrying words

Cognate carry and word material is present, but uerba belongs directly with repulsantes and dicta with referre, and the discourse functions differ. No sufficient evidence of a fixed inherited formula.

search_lead.cognate: ON oddi (oddr, dative singular) / OE ord and ON egio (egg, dative singular eggju) / OE ecge are cognate weapon-part nouns.
search_lead.argument: Both coordinate point and edge as the two means of armed injury: defending a kingdom versus armour blocking entry. Clear inherited Germanic merism worth review; it does not by itself establish PIE phraseology and supplies no second branch slab anchor.

search_lead.cognate: ON bito = bitu, third-person plural preterite of bíta, cognate with OE bītan; the weapon nouns differ.
search_lead.argument: Weapons bite in Norse battle verse and fail to bite in Beowulf. Slab brygiorsverþ needs division into brygior + sverþ; sverþ is the plural subject of bito and vǫlsc its modifier. This is a plausible inherited Germanic weapon metaphor, not evidence here for inheritance across IE branches.

search_lead.cognate: ON yfir and Greek ὑπερ- share the over preposition; no secure hand/hold cognate pairing is asserted.
search_lead.argument: Norse ruler holds a hand over the men of Norway; Homeric gods hold a hand over protected people, including the Trojans who take courage. Matching protection image, but weak lexical anchoring and possible independent or medieval transmitted usage. Review as a semantic lead only, not a reconstructed formula.
